newsitem.title: UK: Pitfalls rife in Eastern European business.
newsitem.headline: Pitfalls rife in Eastern European business.

text.p: If you want to open an office in Eastern Europe or the CIS then try not to choose Ashgabat -- you may have no water and a computer or fridge will blow the electric system, a report published on Wednesday said.
The Economist Intelligence Unit report on the pitfalls of opening and operating offices in Eastern Europe and the CIS confirms some of the old beliefs, but dispels others.
Computer technicians and engineers are still good in Eastern Europe and the younger the staff, the better -- they have had less experience of Soviet doctrines.
But investing in the east can be an expensive business.
Employing reputable security firms and personal drivers are necessities in Moscow and Kiev, the report says, pushing up the cost of any operations there.

Bulgaria has a good cheap supply of office space and few building restrictions boosting its ranking, but in Slovakia the "obstinate and alarmingly secretive bureaucracy" means an expensive office market, the EIU says.

In many countries the race to find multilingual staff has pushed salaries up to Western rates and in Prague foreign companies have devised "golden handcuffs" to stop new recruits taking the training then moving on to higher paid jobs.

Hungary leads the ranking out of 16 countries scoring eight out of 10 on such categories as availability and cost of office space, quality and cost of suitable staff, bureaucracy of registering companies and services such as telephone connections and security.
It is followed by Estonia, Poland and Slovenia. At the bottom end of the table are the former Soviet republics of Belarus, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan last.
